title: The Fruit of Lies
subtitle: On the harvest that grows from trusting one's own way
teaser: Hosea's charge against a working, solvent, well-defended nation is not wickedness. It is management. They had altars, a foreign policy, and not much time left — and the prophet tells them the crop they are standing in is the one they planted.
theme: The harvest a person is standing in is the one that person planted, and self-rule is not neutral ground.
framework: Hosea 10:12-13 — because you have trusted in your own way

modules.passage: For you are fully aware that the Day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. While people are saying, “Peace and security,” destruction will come upon them suddenly, like labor pains on a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.
modules.scriptureContext: Two minutes with the sentence people are saying at the exact moment the passage says they are least safe.

modules.definition: safety, security, certainty — the settled condition of a thing that is not going to give way
modules.usage: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, and the other two uses show its range: Luke opens his Gospel offering Theophilus the asphaleia — the certainty — of what he has been taught, and Acts uses it of a prison locked with all security. So the crowd in this verse is not saying something foolish. They are saying something reasonable. It is the ordinary word for a situation that has been properly seen to.

modules.heading: The Sentence People Say Just Before
modules.content:
Nothing in the verse suggests the people saying "peace and security" are lying, or drunk, or wicked. That is what makes the line land. They are giving an accurate report on their own arrangements. The doors are locked. The accounts balance. The assessment is sound.

The prophets had heard that sentence before. Jeremiah described leaders who dressed the wound of the people with very little care, "saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace at all." Ezekiel described the same habit as whitewashing a flimsy wall — the wall is genuinely whitewashed, and it is genuinely flimsy, and the whitewash is the problem precisely because it works.

What Scripture keeps flagging is not catastrophe arriving out of nowhere. It is the gap between how secure a life feels from inside and what is actually holding it up. A person can be entirely correct about the locks and entirely wrong about the house.

This week begins there and stays there for six days. Not with obvious ruin, but with competence — the quiet, defensible, well-run version of a life that has arranged its own security and no longer needs anyone else to guarantee it. Hosea will call that arrangement by its blunt name tomorrow. Today it is enough to notice how normal it sounds when people say it out loud.

modules.prompt: Everyone has a sentence they say to reassure themselves that things are fundamentally fine. What is it — and when was the last time anyone was allowed to test it?

modules.heading: A Two-Minute Prayer
modules.prayerText: Lord, we are good at reporting on our own arrangements, and we grade ourselves gently. Show us the wall under the whitewash while there is still time to build. Amen.

modules.ctaSubtext: That can be the whole of today. Below, when there is time: a prophet doing agricultural arithmetic on a nation that still had a country, a Hebrew word for road that turns out to be concrete before it is ever moral, and a Russian novelist at the summit of everything he had arranged, hiding a cord from himself.

modules.passage: Sow for yourselves righteousness and reap the fruit of loving devotion; break up your unplowed ground. For it is time to seek the LORD until He comes and sends righteousness upon you like rain. You have plowed wickedness and reaped injustice; you have eaten the fruit of lies. Because you have trusted in your own way and in the multitude of your mighty men,
emphasis: you have eaten the fruit of lies
you have trusted in your own way
modules.scriptureContext: An invitation and an indictment in consecutive breaths, both of them stated as farming.

modules.inlineImageAlt: A wide field split down the middle — deep plowed furrows on one side, hard unbroken crusted ground on the other, with a small figure and a lantern standing at the seam
modules.inlineImageCaption: Hosea's two grounds, side by side: earth that has been broken open, and earth that has not. The prophet is asking which one a life is standing on.

modules.heading: A Nation That Still Had a Country
modules.content:
Hosea prophesied to the northern kingdom in the eighth century before Christ, in the decades running down toward the Assyrian conquest. Samaria fell in 722 or 721 — the sources disagree over which Assyrian king actually took the city — and much of what Hosea says was said to people who still had a functioning country and could not imagine not having one.

That detail matters more than it looks. It is easy to read a prophet as though he were shouting at rubble. He was not. He was shouting at a working economy. The altars in Hosea's Israel were not empty; chapter 10 opens by complaining that the more the land produced, the more altars they built. The army existed. The alliances were being negotiated. From inside, the arrangement was performing.

And into that, Hosea does arithmetic.

Sow righteousness, he says, and reap the fruit of loving devotion. Break up your unplowed ground. Then, without pausing: you have plowed wickedness and reaped injustice, and you have eaten the fruit of lies.

He is not describing two nations. He is describing one nation twice — what it could still plant, and what it has already been harvesting. The whole charge is delivered in the vocabulary of a farm, which is not decoration. Farming is the one human activity where nobody argues about causation. A field returns what went into it, on a delay long enough that the connection can be forgotten and short enough that it cannot be escaped.

And then comes the diagnosis, in a clause that could serve as the epigraph for the entire week.

Because you have trusted in your own way.

modules.definition: a way, road, path — a route as it is actually travelled
modules.usage: Hosea 10:13 has it with a suffix — בְדַרְכְּךָ (vedarkekha), "in your way" — and it is worth resisting the temptation to hear that as an abstraction. The lexicons define derek as a road as trodden. Before it means anything about morality it means something a person can stand on: a route, a direction of travel, the way one actually goes. It appears about 706 times in the Old Testament and six times in Hosea alone.
modules.usageNote: Which is why the accusation is heavier than a comment about opinions. To trust in one's own derek is not to hold private views about God. It is to have chosen a route and to be walking it, with the confidence that walking it will get one somewhere. The prophet's complaint is not that Israel thought wrongly. It is that Israel went somewhere — and that where it went is now growing in the field.

wordByWord.meaning: you trusted — Qal perfect, a completed act, not a drifting mood
in your way — the road as actually walked

relatedWords.meaning: the word behind "the fruit of lies" — its force is a lie that disappoints, a thing that fails the person relying on it, which is precisely what a bad harvest does

modules.content: A field returns what went into it, on a delay long enough that the connection can be forgotten.

modules.heading: The Charge Is Not Wickedness. It Is Management.
modules.content:
There is a way of reading prophetic indictments that keeps them safely away from ordinary life: the people were vicious, the people were idolaters, the people were doing things no reasonable modern person does. Hosea makes that reading difficult, because the sin he names in this verse is a management decision.

Trusted in your own way, and in the multitude of your mighty men. Route and resources. A plan and the means to execute it.

Nothing in that sentence is exotic. It is what any competent person does, and does correctly, in every other area of life. Choose a direction. Secure the assets. Reduce dependence on parties who cannot be controlled. The prophet is not attacking competence — the same book tells them to break up unplowed ground, which is hard, deliberate, skilled work. He is naming the point at which competence quietly became the foundation rather than the tool.

That is the version of this problem that survives into any century. Most people who have drifted from God did not decide against Him. They got good at something. The arrangement held. And the holding of it, over years, made the question of who was underneath it feel abstract.

Calvin located the machinery of this precisely, and he did not locate it in the culture. "The mind of man is," he wrote, "if I may be allowed the expression, a perpetual manufactory of idols." Not a museum of them — a factory, running continuously, in-house. The small gods a person ends up serving are almost never imported. They are produced on site, out of good materials, by someone doing their best.

Which makes Hosea's word for what they have eaten worth a second look. The fruit of lies. The Hebrew behind lies carries the sense of something that fails the one who leans on it — a promise that disappoints when weight comes onto it. It is the exact opposite of the word that closed God's own name on the mountain, which Wednesday's opening verse will come to. One holds. One gives way. Both look identical until the day of the test.

modules.heading: Where This Week Sits in the Story
modules.ancientTruth: Hosea speaks in the last decades of the northern kingdom, with exile close enough to name and not yet close enough to believe. This is the EXILE stretch of God's story — the long consequence arriving on a covenant people who had been warned, and warned kindly, for generations.
modules.modernApplication: The situation the prophet describes is not national collapse. It is the period before it, when everything still works and the warnings sound overstated.
modules.connectionPoint: The week starts here because this is where most people actually live: not in ruin, and not in obedience, but in a functioning arrangement that has quietly stopped needing God to hold it up.
modules.newTestamentEcho: Paul carries Hosea's field logic straight into the churches without changing the metaphor: "Do not be deceived: God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return" (Galatians 6:7). And Peter describes the same condition in Isaiah's older image — "you were like sheep going astray" — before naming the return.

modules.heading: Unplowed Ground
modules.content:
The imperative in the middle of Hosea's invitation is the strangest thing in the passage, and the easiest to read past.

Break up your unplowed ground.

The King James calls it fallow ground, which is closer to how it works. Fallow ground is not wasteland. It is good land that has not been opened. Nothing is wrong with it except that it is closed — crusted over on top from weather and traffic, perfectly capable of growing anything, and currently growing nothing because the surface has never been broken.

So the prophet's instruction to a nation still going about its business is not primarily about behaviour. It is about opening something that has sealed itself.

And that reframes the sin of the chapter. Trusting one's own way is not, in the first instance, a moral failure. It is a closure. A route gets chosen, it works, and over enough years the ground goes hard on top — not through any single decision, but through the ordinary weather of a life that is going fine. The person is not in rebellion. The person is in crust.

This is where the two kinds of reader in this series meet for the first time, and it is worth naming both, because they will both be here all week.

One is managing. Competent, self-directed, and long past the point of needing anyone to underwrite the arrangement. For that reader, Hosea's word is that the arrangement is producing a crop, whether or not anyone is watching the field.

The other has already broken. Someone whose apologies to God have worn out from use, and who has concluded, privately, that the ground is now too hard to be worth opening. For that reader the same verse says something different: fallow ground is not bad ground. It is good ground that is closed, and the instruction given to it is not "replace it" but "break it up."

Both readers are told the same thing about timing, and it is the most hopeful clause in the passage: it is time to seek the LORD until He comes and sends righteousness upon you like rain. The plowing is assigned to the people. The rain is not. Nobody in the history of farming has made it rain. The whole invitation assumes that the part which cannot be manufactured will be given — which is the first appearance in this week of the pattern the rest of it will follow.

modules.heading: The Man at the Summit
modules.content:
By his own reckoning he had assembled everything a life is arranged to get. He was not yet fifty. He had, as he listed it, a good wife who loved him and whom he loved, good children, and a large estate which improved and increased without much effort on his part. He was more respected by his relations than at any previous time. He could consider, without much self-deception, that his name was famous. He was not ill; he could keep up with the peasants at mowing and work ten hours at a stretch without feeling it.

And into the middle of that arrangement, Leo Tolstoy wrote, a question began arriving.

It came while he was thinking about his land in Samara, and it asked: and what next? It came while he was planning his children's education: what for? It came while he was thinking about his own fame, and this time he recorded the exact form of it — "Very well; you will be more famous than Gogol or Pushkin or Shakespeare or Molière, or than all the writers in the world — and what of it?" And he added, plainly: "And I could find no reply at all."

He wrote that his life came to a standstill. He could breathe, eat, drink and sleep, but there was no life in it, because there was no wish whose fulfilment he could consider reasonable. He had walked, he said, until he came to a precipice.

And then a man favoured by fortune began hiding things from himself. He hid a cord, lest he should hang himself from the crosspiece of the partition in the room where he undressed alone every evening. He stopped going out shooting with a gun, lest he should be tempted by so easy a way of ending his life.

"I did not myself know what I wanted," he wrote. "I feared life, desired to escape from it, yet still hoped something of it."
modules.connectionToTheme: Nothing in Tolstoy's account involves a collapse. The estate improved. The books sold. The route he had chosen worked, in every sense a route can work, and it delivered him to a precipice on schedule. This is what Hosea's arithmetic looks like from inside a life rather than from over a nation: the harvest arriving quietly, at the summit, on a man who has done nothing obviously wrong and has trusted entirely in his own way. It should be said that this is a retrospective account, written years later by a man shaping the story toward the conversion his book goes on to argue for. What it is not is a report of failure.

modules.heading: Locked From the Inside
modules.content: C. S. Lewis, arguing about the loss of a single soul, granted the point rather than dodging it: "I willingly believe that the damned are, in one sense, successful, rebels to the end; that the doors of hell are locked on the inside."
modules.historicalContext: The Problem of Pain (1940), chapter VIII. The line is routinely quoted as though it came from The Great Divorce and routinely quoted as a fragment; the full sentence is harder, because it concedes the success before it names the lock.

modules.heading: What the Prophet Does Not Say
modules.content:
Having laid the charge, Hosea does something a modern reader may not expect. He does not tell them to try harder at being Israelite.

The instruction is agricultural and it is limited: sow righteousness, break up the closed ground, seek the LORD. Nowhere is anyone told to generate the rain, and nowhere is anyone told that better effort will produce loving devotion. The verse says they will reap the fruit of loving devotion — the harvest is of a different kind than the sowing, which is a strange thing to say about farming and a very precise thing to say about God.

This is the week's first sight of an asymmetry it will keep returning to. The human side is real work and it is genuinely required. The divine side is not the sum of the human side. Something is given that was not produced.

And it is worth saying clearly what this passage does not permit, because the second kind of reader will reach for it. The invitation is not open indefinitely. "It is time to seek the LORD" is a statement about a window, delivered to people whose country was closer to its end than they believed. Scripture's patience is real and it is not infinite, and pretending otherwise would be exactly the whitewash Ezekiel complained about.

What the passage does permit is more startling than a threat. It assumes that ground which has gone hard can be opened. It assumes that a nation currently eating the fruit of lies is still being handed a plough. The charge and the invitation are in the same two verses, in that order, addressed to the same people — which means Hosea considered a hardened people worth instructing, and considered the instruction worth giving before anything had changed.

modules.passage: There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
modules.scriptureContext: The same Hebrew word — derek, a way — with the whole problem stated in a single clause. Proverbs thought the sentence important enough to print twice; it appears again, verbatim, at 16:25.

modules.prompt: Hosea's charge is aimed at a working arrangement, not a ruined one. Where has a life gone right in a way that has quietly made God optional?
additionalQuestions: Fallow ground is good ground that has closed over. What in a person's life is not bad, only crusted — and what would breaking it open actually involve this week?
The passage assigns the plowing and promises the rain. Where has someone been trying to manufacture the rain?
Tolstoy's question was 'and what of it?' at the summit of everything he had built. What is currently being built that would not survive that question?

modules.heading: A Practice for Today
modules.instruction: A breath prayer, using Hosea's own two halves. Six slow breaths, no more. It works best somewhere with a door.

steps.title: In
steps.description: Breathing in, silently: I have trusted in my own way.

steps.title: Out
steps.description: Breathing out, silently: it is time to seek the LORD.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.description: Six times, slowly. Do not add anything to it and do not try to feel something. The words are doing the work; the exercise is only holding still long enough to hear them.

modules.heading: Two Verses, in Order
modules.content:
The order of Hosea's two verses is worth keeping, because most people would have written them the other way round.

First the invitation. Sow, reap, break up the ground, seek Him, and rain will come. Then the indictment: you have plowed wickedness and reaped injustice and eaten the fruit of lies, because you trusted your own way.

A prophet building a case would put the charge first and the offer second, as a reward for having taken the charge seriously. Hosea does not. He opens with the plough in their hands and the promise of rain, and only then explains what the field currently contains.

Which is a small thing and a revealing one. The invitation is not what a person earns by admitting the diagnosis. It is what is already extended while the diagnosis is still true.

Augustine, opening the book that would become his confession, addressed God with the sentence that has followed the church ever since: "Thou awakest us to delight in Thy praise; for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." He wrote it as a man looking back at exactly the condition this week begins in — a life that worked, running on its own way, and unable to explain why it would not settle.

The restlessness is not the punishment. In Hosea's terms it is closer to the weather that cracks the crust.

Six days remain in this reading. Tomorrow it goes further back than Hosea, to the first time anyone chose their own way and to what was actually being reached for. But today ends where the prophet ended it: with a field that is telling the truth about what was planted in it, and a plough that has not been taken away.

modules.heading: Closing Prayer
modules.prayerText: Lord of the harvest, we have been careful about the wrong things. We secured the route and the resources and called it wisdom, and the ground went hard on top while everything was going well. We have eaten the fruit of lies and found it filling. Break open what has closed. Give us the honesty to look at the field and say what is actually growing there, without softening it and without despairing over it. And send the rain, which we have never once been able to make. It is time to seek You. We are seeking You. Amen.
modules.breathPrayer: Breathing in: I have trusted my own way. Breathing out: it is time to seek the LORD.

modules.heading: Today's Commitment
modules.commitment: I will name one place where my own competence has quietly become my foundation, and I will break the ground there this week instead of admiring the crust.
leavingAtCross: The report I keep filing on my own security
The assumption that a working arrangement is a right one
The idea that hard ground is finished ground
receivingFromCross: A plough still in my hands after the charge has been read
A promise of rain I was never able to manufacture
An invitation extended before anything about me had changed

modules.heading: One Question
modules.question: What does Hosea mean by telling the people to "break up your unplowed ground"?
options: To abandon their land and start again somewhere else
To work harder at religious observance until God is satisfied
To open ground that is good but has closed over — the problem is a hardened surface, not bad soil
To destroy the altars they had built
modules.explanation: Fallow ground is not wasteland. It is capable land whose surface has crusted, and the instruction is to open it. That is why the charge and the invitation can sit in the same two verses: the people are hardened, not written off, and the plough is handed to them before anything has changed.

modules.heading: The Voice Behind Today
modules.name: Hosea son of Beeri
modules.era: eighth century BC, the northern kingdom of Israel
modules.bio: A prophet whose own marriage became the sign he was sent to deliver. He spoke into the last decades of the northern kingdom, during a stretch of relative prosperity, to people who still had a country. Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 or 721 BC.
modules.keyQuote: Sow for yourselves righteousness and reap the fruit of loving devotion; break up your unplowed ground.
modules.lessonForUs: Hosea is the prophet who will not let covenant be discussed as a legal matter. He turns every charge into either farming or marriage — two things that cannot be conducted at arm's length — and that is why his indictment of self-rule lands somewhere colder than an argument would.

modules.videoTitle: A World of Idols – Timothy Keller [Sermon]
modules.videoCaption: A longer go-deeper for later in the day: why the human heart keeps manufacturing its own gods, and what that has to do with things going well.

modules.heading: Sources & Further Study

relatedScriptures.text: The same field logic two chapters earlier: "For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind."
Two evils named together — forsaking the fountain, and digging cisterns that cannot hold water. Self-supply as the second half of the problem.
Hosea's agriculture carried into the church without altering the metaphor, and ending in an encouragement rather than a threat.
"Let the wicked man forsake his own way" — the same word, the same instruction, and the reason attached: God's ways are not ours.
The refrain that ends Judges, describing the condition Hosea is diagnosing: "every man did that which was right in his own eyes."

resources.title: Leo Tolstoy, A Confession, chapter IV
resources.description: Source of today's story and every quoted phrase in it, verbatim from Aylmer Maude's translation (A Confession and What I Believe, The World's Classics, Oxford University Press, 1921, pp. 21-22). Maude's word is "a cord," not the "rope" of most retellings. It circulated abroad in the mid-1880s. Free at archive.org.

resources.title: C. S. Lewis, The Problem of Pain (1940), chapter VIII, "Hell"
resources.description: Source of the quotation on the doors of hell, verbatim from the Macmillan (New York) printing, p. 81. Frequently misattributed to The Great Divorce.

resources.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion (1559), Book I, ch. XI, sec. VIII
resources.description: Quoted here in John Allen's 1813 translation — "a perpetual manufactory of idols." The more famous "perpetual factory of idols" belongs to the 1960 Battles translation, and Beveridge has "perpetual forge." All three render the same passage.

resources.title: Augustine, Confessions, Book I, ch. 1
resources.description: Quoted verbatim in E. B. Pusey's translation, which reads "our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." The familiar "our hearts are restless until they rest in you" belongs to later translators. Free at gutenberg.org.

resources.title: Hebrew data
resources.description: derek (H1870) — "a road as trodden"; about 706 OT occurrences, 6 in Hosea; in Hosea 10:13 it carries a second-person suffix, vedarkekha. batach (H982), "you trusted," is a Qal perfect. kachash (H3585) underlies "the fruit of lies"; its better-attested force is a lie that disappoints the one relying on it. asphaleia (G803) occurs 3 times in the New Testament (Luke 1:4; Acts 5:23; 1 Thessalonians 5:3).

modules.forDeeperStudy: Read Hosea 10 whole, then Hosea 8:7, then Galatians 6:7-9. The question to carry through all three: in each passage, what is assigned to the farmer, and what is not — and which of the two has been the source of the most exhaustion?
